newsitem.title: UK: Funds seek extra value from stretched stocks.
newsitem.headline: Funds seek extra value from stretched stocks.

text.p: Global fund managers are looking to squeeze further value out of major equity markets amid concerns that a choppy six months may lie in wait for investors.

A Reuter survey of mostly British-based fund managers showed underweighting of the U.S. equity market was continuing across the board, although many managers saw liquidity supporting further gains in the short term.

"We are increasingly aware we are pushing into valuation levels that make this bull run stack up alongside the biggest that we have seen through the century," said Matthew Merritt, strategist at ING Barings.
The respondents were polled before the Dow broke through 8,000 points on Wednesday.
Merritt sees upside in the U.S. limited to about 950 on the S&P 500 and 8,300 to 8,400 on the Dow. "But beyond there we really start pushing into heavily overvalued territory."
Analysts generally expect the U.S. to run further, but they are seeing relative value in other areas.

The poll showed some managers pushing up their U.S. allocations, but remaining underweight, with an average allocation of 27.5 percent to the U.S and Canada against 26.5 in June. Cash was at its lowest level since April at 4.1 percent as managers looked to remain invested.

Andrew Hutchings, global fund co-ordinator at GT Global, said the group had raised its U.S. exposure from a deep underweighting amid expectations that inflationary pressures will remain limited despite faster than expected growth. But the group was still underweight relative to benchmarks.
A recent survey of U.S. fund managers by Merrill Lynch showed managers were more bullish about the outlook for U.S. equities as prospects for a hike in interest rates receded.

The Reuter poll showed Asia ex-Japan allocations were cut in July while Latin America and other emerging markets picked up further flows. The poll showed a 7.7 percent allocation to Latam and other emerging markets -- more than double the 3.5 percent seen at the start of the year.
ING Barings is running overweight in Europe and the UK, with the UK offering possibly the most reasonable valuations.
Merritt said the concerns about the UK election that had led many players to underweight the UK for some time had been overblown.
When looking at global developed market valuations, "all of the major markets are pushing well above longer term average price/equity ratios."
"We are eking out the last bit of value in developed markets and in that context the UK actually stacks up as one of the markets that is much more in neutral valuation territory," he said.

Merritt said the issue with continental Europe was when to lighten the position. A weaker mark, strong domestic liquidity flowing to equity markets and a focus on shareholder value had been offering support.

"The whole issue is when do we start to lighten that position out, and the first prospects that we see of a greater degree of mark strength will provide one of the catalysts which will start getting us moving funds out of that area."
Merritt said he was biased to emerging markets, largely due to lower valuations which provide the scope for more significant upside.

Hutchings said European markets had performed well in local currency terms and had probably now discounted most of the good news that could be expected from a cyclical upturn in economic growth and earnings.

"The situation is really a reflection of the fact we have been underweight and that we are relatively more bullish on the U.S. by comparison with the other developed markets of the world than we had been six months ago."
In bonds, the U.S. remained the major play. "That is really where the greatest degree of value will be," said Merritt. He said the uncertainty over EMU was pushing funds into core Europe.

"The house view is that EMU happens (and) it will be on narrow terms rather than soft. That clearly reflects the scope for spread convergence for the high yielders looks relatively limited, but on a 12 month view you will probably see bund yields backing up marginally from here," he said.
"But that still suggests there is a greater degree of comfort in the core."
The survey showed managers upping their U.S. allocation in the global bond fund to 33.9 percent from 31.3 percent.
Nick Knight, global strategist at Nomura International, said a dichotomy was developing in bond markets between the U.S. and Europe, with the U.S. proving a haven amid EMU uncertainty.
"The U.S. should be supported by a strong dollar and Europe should be undermined by a weak mark," he said.
